items.text: I'm so sorry to hear that
items.form: I'm so sorry to hear that
items.meaning: Expresses sympathy and regret upon receiving bad news.
items.example: Oh, I'm so sorry to hear that your project didn't get approved after all your hard work.
items.plain: Oh, I feel bad that your project didn't get approved after all your hard work.
items.note: A very common and sincere way to express sympathy for someone's misfortune or disappointment.

items.meaning: Expresses mild disappointment or regret about a situation.
items.example: That's a shame you won't be able to join us for dinner tonight, we'll miss you.
items.plain: It's disappointing you won't be able to join us for dinner tonight, we'll miss you.
items.note: Used for minor disappointments or when something good doesn't happen. Less intense than "tragedy".

items.meaning: Expresses sympathy for someone experiencing a minor difficulty or discomfort.
items.example: You had to work late again? Poor you, that sounds really exhausting.
items.plain: You had to work late again? I feel bad for you, that sounds really exhausting.
items.note: A casual, empathetic phrase, often used among friends or close colleagues. Can be slightly teasing if the problem is very minor.

items.meaning: Shows empathy by acknowledging the difficulty of someone's situation.
items.example: Losing your main client after so many years, it must be tough to deal with that.
items.plain: Losing your main client after so many years, I imagine that's very difficult to deal with.
items.note: A thoughtful way to express understanding without claiming to fully know their experience.

items.meaning: Expresses empathy by indicating shared experience or understanding of emotions.
items.example: When my laptop crashed last week, I know how you feel about losing all that unsaved work.
items.plain: When my laptop crashed last week, I understand your frustration about losing all that unsaved work.
items.note: Can be comforting, but ensure you genuinely relate to avoid sounding dismissive.

items.meaning: Expresses empathy by acknowledging the difficulty or intensity of someone's experience.
items.example: After working on that report for months, having it rejected, I can only imagine how frustrating that must be.
items.plain: After working on that report for months, having it rejected, I understand how frustrating that must be.
items.note: A polite and sincere way to show you understand the gravity of a situation, even if you haven't experienced it.

items.meaning: Expresses strong sympathy or dismay at bad news or a negative situation.
items.example: Oh, that's really awful that your flight was cancelled and you missed the conference.
items.plain: Oh, it's terrible that your flight was cancelled and you missed the conference.
items.note: A direct and common expression of sympathy or shock at something negative.

items.meaning: Expresses sincere regret or apology, often for something significant.
items.example: I'm truly sorry for the misunderstanding during the meeting; I didn't mean to cause any offense.
items.plain: I sincerely regret the misunderstanding during the meeting; I didn't mean to cause any offense.
items.note: A more formal or emphatic apology than "I'm sorry," conveying deeper regret.

items.meaning: Expresses empathy and acknowledges the challenging nature of someone's circumstances.
items.example: Having to choose between two job offers in different cities, what a difficult situation to be in.
items.plain: Having to choose between two job offers in different cities, that's a very challenging situation.
items.note: A common way to show understanding and compassion when someone is facing a tough choice or problem.

items.meaning: Expresses strong delight and happiness upon hearing positive information.
items.example: You got the promotion? That's wonderful news, congratulations!
items.plain: You got the promotion? That's excellent information, congratulations!
items.note: A very common and enthusiastic way to react to good news.

items.meaning: Expresses genuine happiness and congratulations for someone else's success or good fortune.
items.example: I'm so pleased for you that your visa application was finally approved after all that waiting.
items.plain: I'm very happy for you that your visa application was finally approved after all that waiting.
items.note: A warm and personal expression of joy for another person's positive outcome.

items.meaning: Expresses enthusiasm and anticipation about something new or interesting.
items.example: You're moving to a new country next month? How exciting, I can't wait to hear all about it!
items.plain: You're moving to a new country next month? That's very thrilling, I can't wait to hear all about it!
items.note: A common, informal way to show enthusiasm. Can be used as a standalone exclamation.

items.meaning: Expresses extreme joy and contentment about a situation.
items.example: With the project finished ahead of schedule and under budget, I couldn't be happier.
items.plain: With the project finished ahead of schedule and under budget, I am extremely happy.
items.note: A strong, emphatic way to convey maximum happiness.

items.meaning: Expresses formal or sincere happiness about information received.
items.example: I'm delighted to hear that your recovery is going so well after the surgery.
items.plain: I'm very happy to hear that your recovery is going so well after the surgery.
items.note: A slightly more formal or considered way to express happiness than "That's wonderful news."

items.meaning: Expresses pleasant astonishment and happiness at an unexpected positive event.
items.example: Oh, you brought me flowers? What a lovely surprise, thank you so much!
items.plain: Oh, you brought me flowers? That's a very pleasant unexpected gift, thank you so much!
items.note: A warm and appreciative reaction to an unexpected positive gesture or event.

items.meaning: Expresses intense excitement and happiness on behalf of someone else.
items.example: You got accepted into your dream university! I'm thrilled for you, that's fantastic!
items.plain: You got accepted into your dream university! I'm very excited and happy for you, that's fantastic!
items.note: A strong, enthusiastic expression of happiness for another person's good fortune.

items.meaning: Expresses mild irritation or frustration about a minor inconvenience.
items.example: The train is delayed again? That's a bit annoying, I have a meeting in twenty minutes.
items.plain: The train is delayed again? That's slightly irritating, I have a meeting in twenty minutes.
items.note: A common, understated way to express mild frustration without being overly dramatic.

items.meaning: Expresses exasperation, impatience, or mild annoyance.
items.example: Oh, for goodness sake, the printer's jammed again right when I need to print these documents!
items.plain: Oh, this is frustrating, the printer's jammed again right when I need to print these documents!
items.note: A common exclamation of frustration, often used when something goes wrong repeatedly or unexpectedly.

items.text: You've got to be kidding me
items.form: You've got to be kidding me
items.meaning: Expresses disbelief, surprise, or annoyance at something unexpected or unreasonable.
items.example: They cancelled our reservation at the last minute? You've got to be kidding me, we booked weeks ago!
items.plain: They cancelled our reservation at the last minute? I can't believe it, we booked weeks ago!
items.note: A strong, informal expression of disbelief or frustration. Can be used humorously or seriously.

items.meaning: Expresses that something is excessive, unreasonable, or overwhelming.
items.example: Expecting us to work weekends without extra pay, that's a bit much, don't you think?
items.plain: Expecting us to work weekends without extra pay, that's unreasonable, don't you think?
items.note: Used to politely suggest that a demand or situation is unfair or goes beyond what is acceptable.

items.meaning: Expresses strong annoyance or disappointment when something prevents progress or success.
items.example: The constant technical issues with the new software, that's really frustrating for the whole team.
items.plain: The constant technical issues with the new software, that's very annoying for the whole team.
items.note: A direct and common way to express strong frustration.

items.text: I can't believe it happened again
items.form: I can't believe it happened again
items.meaning: Expresses exasperation or disbelief when a negative event recurs.
items.example: The internet went down during our video call. I can't believe it happened again!
items.plain: The internet went down during our video call. I'm so annoyed it recurred!
items.note: Used when a recurring problem causes annoyance or disappointment.

items.meaning: Expresses that a situation is less than perfect or has drawbacks, often politely.
items.example: Having to reschedule the meeting at such short notice, it's not ideal for everyone's calendars.
items.plain: Having to reschedule the meeting at such short notice, it's inconvenient for everyone's calendars.
items.note: A polite and understated way to express dissatisfaction or acknowledge a less-than-perfect situation.

items.meaning: Expresses resignation or mild annoyance when something predictable but undesirable occurs.
items.example: The bus is late again. That's just typical, it always happens when I'm in a hurry.
items.plain: The bus is late again. That's predictable, it always happens when I'm in a hurry.
items.note: Used when a recurring negative event confirms a pattern, often with a sigh of resignation.

items.text: I'm a bit fed up with it
items.form: I'm a bit fed up with it
items.meaning: Expresses mild to moderate annoyance or boredom with a recurring situation.
items.example: This constant noise from the construction site, I'm a bit fed up with it now.
items.plain: This constant noise from the construction site, I'm quite annoyed by it now.
items.note: An informal way to say you've had enough of something annoying.

items.meaning: Expresses sudden comfort and ease after a period of worry or stress.
items.example: The test results came back negative. What a relief, I was so worried!
items.plain: The test results came back negative. That's a great comfort, I was so worried!
items.note: A very common and emphatic exclamation of relief.

items.meaning: Expresses relief or gratitude that something bad was avoided or something good happened.
items.example: Thank goodness the rain held off until after our outdoor event finished.
items.plain: I'm grateful the rain held off until after our outdoor event finished.
items.note: A common, slightly informal expression of relief, often used as an exclamation.

items.meaning: Expresses personal feeling of comfort and ease after a period of anxiety.
items.example: When I heard the plane landed safely, I was so relieved.
items.plain: When I heard the plane landed safely, I felt a great sense of comfort.
items.note: A direct and common way to express personal relief.

items.text: That's a weight off my mind
items.form: that's a weight off my mind
items.meaning: Expresses great relief that a worry or burden has been removed.
items.example: Knowing the children are safely home, that's a weight off my mind.
items.plain: Knowing the children are safely home, I feel much less worried.
items.note: A common idiom to describe feeling relieved after a concern is resolved.

items.meaning: Expresses relief after a moment of anxiety caused by someone or something.
items.example: When you didn't answer your phone, you had me worried there for a moment.
items.plain: When you didn't answer your phone, I was worried for a moment.
items.note: A common, informal phrase used to express relief after a brief scare.

items.meaning: Expresses happiness or relief about information received.
items.example: I'm glad to hear that your presentation went well this morning.
items.plain: I'm happy that your presentation went well this morning.
items.note: A versatile and polite way to respond positively to news.

items.meaning: Expresses appreciation for useful or reassuring information.
items.example: So the deadline has been extended? That's good to know, I was feeling a bit rushed.
items.plain: So the deadline has been extended? That information is useful, I was feeling a bit rushed.
items.note: A common, practical response to receiving helpful or comforting information.

items.meaning: Expresses strong surprise or disbelief, often in an informal context.
items.example: You won the lottery? You're kidding me, that's incredible!
items.plain: You won the lottery? I don't believe it, that's incredible!
items.note: A very common, informal expression of surprise. Can be positive or negative.

items.meaning: Expresses strong disbelief or surprise, often informally.
items.example: They offered you the job on the spot? No way, that's amazing!
items.plain: They offered you the job on the spot? I can't believe it, that's amazing!
items.note: A very informal and emphatic expression of disbelief or astonishment.

items.meaning: Expresses strong surprise, disbelief, or astonishment at an event or news.
items.example: I can't believe it's already been five years since we started this company.
items.plain: I'm so surprised it's already been five years since we started this company.
items.note: A versatile phrase for expressing strong emotion, positive or negative, about something unexpected.

items.meaning: Expresses mild surprise or acknowledgement that something was not anticipated.
items.example: They decided to close the branch office? That's unexpected, I thought it was doing well.
items.plain: They decided to close the branch office? I didn't expect that, I thought it was doing well.
items.note: A polite and neutral way to express surprise.

items.meaning: Expresses disbelief or surprise, asking for confirmation of surprising news.
items.example: They're moving the deadline forward by a week? Are you serious?
items.plain: They're moving the deadline forward by a week? Is that true?
items.note: A common, informal way to check if surprising information is true.

items.meaning: Expresses extreme surprise, shock, or overwhelming emotion, leaving one unable to speak.
items.example: When they announced my name for the award, I was completely speechless.
items.plain: When they announced my name for the award, I was so surprised I couldn't speak.
items.note: Used when an event or news is so overwhelming that it renders one temporarily unable to respond verbally.

items.meaning: Expresses surprise, shock, or momentary confusion, often in a negative sense.
items.example: Her sudden resignation really took me aback; I had no idea she was unhappy.
items.plain: Her sudden resignation really surprised me; I had no idea she was unhappy.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to express surprise, often implying a moment of disorientation.

items.meaning: Expresses surprise, astonishment, or mild indignation at something unexpected.
items.example: Well, I never, they actually finished the project a day early!
items.plain: I'm surprised, they actually finished the project a day early!
items.note: An older, but still used, informal expression of surprise, often with a hint of mild shock or admiration.

items.meaning: Expresses a moderate level of astonishment or unexpectedness.
items.example: Finding out they're opening a new office overseas, that's quite a surprise.
items.plain: Finding out they're opening a new office overseas, that's rather unexpected.
items.note: A polite and common way to acknowledge something unexpected.

items.meaning: Expresses understanding or agreement with someone's point of view or explanation.
items.example: Ah, I see what you mean about the new software update; it does make things more complicated.
items.plain: Ah, I understand your point about the new software update; it does make things more complicated.
items.note: A common phrase to indicate comprehension and often, agreement.

items.meaning: Expresses acceptance or acknowledgement of a point, even if not fully agreeing.
items.example: You want to leave early to avoid traffic? Fair enough, that makes sense.
items.plain: You want to leave early to avoid traffic? I accept your reason, that makes sense.
items.note: A common, informal way to concede a point or acknowledge a reasonable argument.

items.meaning: Expresses understanding and logical agreement with an explanation or idea.
items.example: Oh, so the delay was due to a technical issue. That makes sense now.
items.plain: Oh, so the delay was due to a technical issue. I understand that now.
items.note: A very common and useful phrase to indicate comprehension and logical acceptance.

items.meaning: Expresses gratitude or acknowledgement of someone's effort, offer, or understanding.
items.example: Thank you for offering to help with the presentation; I appreciate that.
items.plain: Thank you for offering to help with the presentation; I am grateful for that.
items.note: A polite and common way to express thanks or acknowledge a kind gesture.

items.meaning: Expresses reluctant or hesitant agreement, often implying a lack of strong conviction.
items.example: Should we just reschedule for next week? I suppose so, there's no other option.
items.plain: Should we just reschedule for next week? I guess so, there's no other option.
items.note: A common way to agree without much enthusiasm or when there's no better alternative.

items.meaning: Expresses polite disagreement or a gentle correction of someone's statement.
items.example: You think the new policy is a complete disaster? I wouldn't say that, it has some benefits.
items.plain: You think the new policy is a complete disaster? I disagree, it has some benefits.
items.note: A diplomatic way to express disagreement without being confrontational.

items.meaning: Expresses polite doubt or disagreement with a statement or idea.
items.example: He thinks the project will be finished by Friday, but I'm not sure about that.
items.plain: He thinks the project will be finished by Friday, but I doubt it.
items.note: A common and polite way to express uncertainty or mild disagreement.

items.meaning: Introduces a frank or sincere opinion, often one that might be slightly negative or surprising.
items.example: To be honest, I found the workshop a bit boring, even though it was well-organized.
items.plain: Frankly, I found the workshop a bit boring, even though it was well-organized.
items.note: A common discourse marker used to introduce a candid opinion.

items.meaning: Introduces a strong opinion or observation, often one that is important or surprising.
items.example: I have to say, your presentation was incredibly clear and persuasive.
items.plain: I must state, your presentation was incredibly clear and persuasive.
items.note: A common way to introduce a strong, often positive, personal observation or opinion.

items.meaning: Introduces an acknowledgement or confession, often of something slightly unexpected or reluctant.
items.example: I must admit, I was skeptical at first, but the new system is actually quite efficient.
items.plain: I confess, I was skeptical at first, but the new system is actually quite efficient.
items.note: Used to introduce a concession or a slightly surprising personal admission.

items.meaning: Expresses understanding and shared experience with someone's feelings or situation.
items.example: You're feeling overwhelmed with deadlines? I can relate to that, I've been there many times.
items.plain: You're feeling overwhelmed with deadlines? I understand that feeling, I've been there many times.
items.note: A common and empathetic way to show you understand someone's experience because you've had a similar one.

items.meaning: Expresses agreement and acknowledgement of a valid or insightful argument.
items.example: You're right, we should consider the long-term costs. That's a good point.
items.plain: You're right, we should consider the long-term costs. That's a valid argument.
items.note: A common and polite way to acknowledge the validity of someone's contribution to a discussion.

items.meaning: Expresses strong agreement with someone's opinion or stance.
items.example: I think we need to prioritize quality over speed, and I'm with you on that.
items.plain: I think we need to prioritize quality over speed, and I agree with you.
items.note: An informal but common way to express full agreement.

items.meaning: Expresses complete and emphatic agreement with someone's statement.
items.example: You're absolutely right about the need for better communication; I couldn't agree more.
items.plain: You're absolutely right about the need for better communication; I completely agree.
items.note: A strong and common way to express full agreement.

items.meaning: Expresses mild worry or apprehension about a situation.
items.example: The recent drop in sales, I'm a bit concerned about its impact on our quarterly targets.
items.plain: The recent drop in sales, I'm slightly worried about its impact on our quarterly targets.
items.note: A polite and common way to express mild worry without causing alarm.

items.meaning: Expresses that a situation or piece of news causes anxiety or concern.
items.example: The sudden increase in global fuel prices, that's worrying for our shipping costs.
items.plain: The sudden increase in global fuel prices, that causes anxiety for our shipping costs.
items.note: A direct and common way to describe something as a cause for concern.

items.meaning: Expresses concern and a wish for a positive outcome in a potentially difficult situation.
items.example: Your colleague left the meeting looking upset; I hope everything's okay with her.
items.plain: Your colleague left the meeting looking upset; I wish she is fine.
items.note: A common and empathetic way to express concern for someone's well-being.

items.meaning: Expresses personal anxiety or concern regarding a specific issue or person.
items.example: I'm worried about the upcoming budget cuts and how they'll affect our department.
items.plain: I'm anxious about the upcoming budget cuts and how they'll affect our department.
items.note: A direct way to state a personal concern.

items.meaning: Expresses that a situation causes some degree of anxiety or concern.
items.example: The lack of progress on the new project, it's a bit worrying, to be honest.
items.plain: The lack of progress on the new project, it causes some anxiety, to be honest.
items.note: Similar to "I'm a bit concerned," but focuses on the situation itself rather than personal feeling.

items.meaning: Expresses mild disappointment or regret about an outcome.
items.example: The sales figures for this quarter are lower than expected. That's a bit disappointing.
items.plain: The sales figures for this quarter are lower than expected. That's slightly disheartening.
items.note: A common and polite way to express mild disappointment.

items.meaning: Expresses regret or mild disappointment about a situation.
items.example: It's a shame we couldn't get tickets for the concert, it sold out so fast.
items.plain: It's disappointing we couldn't get tickets for the concert, it sold out so fast.
items.note: Very similar to "That's a shame," used interchangeably.

items.meaning: Expresses a past expectation or desire that was not met, implying disappointment.
items.example: I was hoping for a quick resolution to the issue, but it seems it will take longer.
items.plain: I expected a quick resolution to the issue, but it seems it will take longer.
items.note: A polite way to express disappointment by stating a previous, unfulfilled hope.

items.meaning: Expresses that a plan or attempt was unsuccessful, often implying mild disappointment.
items.example: We tried to merge the two departments, but it didn't quite work out as planned.
items.plain: We tried to merge the two departments, but it wasn't successful as planned.
items.note: A common, understated way to describe a failed attempt or plan.

items.meaning: A polite apology for breaking into someone's conversation or activity.
items.example: I'm sorry to interrupt, but I have an urgent call coming in.
items.plain: Please excuse me for interrupting, but I have an urgent call coming in.
items.note: A standard polite phrase for interrupting.

items.meaning: A polite apology for disturbing someone, often before making a request.
items.example: I'm sorry to bother you, but could you help me with this spreadsheet?
items.plain: Please excuse me for disturbing you, but could you help me with this spreadsheet?
items.note: A common polite opening when you need to ask someone for something or interrupt their work.

items.meaning: Expresses an apology for causing something to be late.
items.example: I'm sorry for the delay in sending the report; I had some technical issues.
items.plain: I apologize for the lateness in sending the report; I had some technical issues.
items.note: A standard and polite apology for lateness.

items.meaning: Expresses an apology for causing misunderstanding or lack of clarity.
items.example: I'm sorry for the confusion regarding the meeting time; I sent out the wrong calendar invite.
items.plain: I apologize for the misunderstanding regarding the meeting time; I sent out the wrong calendar invite.
items.note: A polite and professional apology when a mistake has led to misunderstanding.

items.meaning: Expresses an apology for causing trouble or difficulty for someone.
items.example: We had to cancel the event at short notice, and I'm sorry for the inconvenience this caused.
items.plain: We had to cancel the event at short notice, and I apologize for the trouble this caused.
items.note: A standard, polite, and often formal apology for causing trouble.

items.meaning: Introduces bad news or an unwelcome statement, softening the impact.
items.example: I'm sorry to say that your application was not successful this time.
items.plain: I regret to inform you that your application was not successful this time.
items.note: A polite and common way to deliver negative news.

items.meaning: A polite way to ask for permission or to soften a potentially intrusive action.
items.example: I hope you don't mind, but I've already ordered coffee for everyone.
items.plain: I hope you are okay with this, but I've already ordered coffee for everyone.
items.note: Used to check if an action is acceptable, often when it's already been done or is about to be.

items.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to give a negative answer.
items.example: Can you still make it to the workshop tomorrow? I'm afraid not, I have another commitment.
items.plain: Can you still make it to the workshop tomorrow? Unfortunately no, I have another commitment.
items.note: A common, polite, and slightly apologetic way to say "no."

items.meaning: A polite and slightly regretful way to give an affirmative answer to unwelcome news.
items.example: Is the meeting really going to run over time? I'm afraid so, we have a lot to cover.
items.plain: Is the meeting really going to run over time? Unfortunately yes, we have a lot to cover.
items.note: A common, polite, and slightly apologetic way to say "yes" to something undesirable.

items.meaning: Expresses sincere gratitude and appreciation for someone's generosity or thoughtfulness.
items.example: Thank you for helping me move all those boxes; that's really kind of you.
items.plain: Thank you for helping me move all those boxes; you are very thoughtful.
items.note: A warm and common way to express appreciation for a helpful or generous act.

items.meaning: Expresses being deeply moved emotionally by someone's kindness, generosity, or words.
items.example: Your thoughtful card and flowers, I'm truly touched by your support during this time.
items.plain: Your thoughtful card and flowers, I'm deeply moved by your support during this time.
items.note: A sincere expression of gratitude and emotional appreciation.

items.meaning: Expresses regret or sadness about a missed opportunity or an unfortunate situation.
items.example: It's a pity we didn't get to see the exhibition before it closed last week.
items.plain: It's regrettable we didn't get to see the exhibition before it closed last week.
items.note: A common way to express mild regret or sadness. Similar to "It's a shame."

items.meaning: Expresses regret or disappointment about an unfortunate event or missed opportunity.
items.example: What a shame that the outdoor concert was cancelled due to the heavy rain.
items.plain: It's disappointing that the outdoor concert was cancelled due to the heavy rain.
items.note: A common expression of regret, often for something that could have been good but didn't happen.

items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to assist after providing aid.
items.example: I'm glad we could help you sort out the technical issues with your presentation.
items.plain: I'm happy that we were able to assist you with the technical issues with your presentation.
items.note: A polite and common phrase used by someone who has provided assistance.

items.meaning: Expresses genuine joy and congratulations for someone else's success or good fortune.
items.example: You passed your final exams with flying colours! I'm so happy for you!
items.plain: You passed your final exams with flying colours! I'm very pleased for you!
items.note: A warm and common way to express joy for another person's positive outcome.

items.meaning: Expresses strong enthusiasm and approval for something positive.
items.example: The new project proposal got approved? That's fantastic!
items.plain: The new project proposal got approved? That's excellent!
items.note: A common, informal exclamation of delight or approval.

items.meaning: Expresses intense excitement and happiness about a personal event or news.
items.example: I'm absolutely thrilled that my book was finally published after years of work.
items.plain: I'm extremely excited that my book was finally published after years of work.
items.note: A strong, emphatic way to convey personal joy and excitement.

items.meaning: Expresses comfort and ease upon receiving reassuring news.
items.example: What a relief to hear that your surgery went well and you're recovering quickly.
items.plain: It's a great comfort to hear that your surgery went well and you're recovering quickly.
items.note: A common way to express relief when hearing positive news after a period of worry.

items.meaning: Expresses relief that a difficult or unpleasant situation has ended.
items.example: After weeks of intense negotiations, I'm glad that's over and we can move forward.
items.plain: After weeks of intense negotiations, I'm happy it's finished and we can move forward.
items.note: A common, informal expression of relief after a challenging period.

items.meaning: Expresses happiness and mild astonishment at an unexpected positive event.
items.example: Oh, you finished the report early? That's a pleasant surprise!
items.plain: Oh, you finished the report early? That's a nice unexpected event!
items.note: A polite and common way to react positively to something unexpected.

items.meaning: Expresses a moderate level of astonishment or unexpectedness.
items.example: I'm quite surprised by the sudden change in management; it was very quick.
items.plain: I'm rather astonished by the sudden change in management; it was very quick.
items.note: A polite and common way to express surprise without being overly dramatic.

items.meaning: Expresses surprise or ignorance about a piece of information.
items.example: You're fluent in Japanese? I had no idea, that's impressive!
items.plain: You're fluent in Japanese? I didn't know that, that's impressive!
items.note: A common, informal way to express surprise at new information.

items.meaning: Expresses surprise or mild disbelief that one was unaware of certain information.
items.example: They're closing the cafeteria next month? That's news to me!
items.plain: They're closing the cafeteria next month? I didn't know that!
items.note: A common, informal phrase indicating that information is new and surprising to the speaker.

items.meaning: Expresses being unexpectedly astonished or shocked by an event.
items.example: When they announced the unexpected bonus, I was taken by surprise.
items.plain: When they announced the unexpected bonus, I was unexpectedly astonished.
items.note: A slightly more formal way to express being caught off guard by something unexpected.

items.meaning: Expresses understanding of the reasons behind someone's feelings or actions.
items.example: You're upset about the decision? I can see why, it affects your team directly.
items.plain: You're upset about the decision? I understand the reasons, it affects your team directly.
items.note: A common, empathetic phrase to show understanding of someone's perspective.

items.meaning: Expresses that someone's feelings or actions are reasonable and easy to comprehend.
items.example: You're tired after working all weekend? That's understandable.
items.plain: You're tired after working all weekend? That's reasonable.
items.note: A polite and common way to validate someone's feelings or situation.

items.meaning: Expresses understanding of someone's point or argument, often informally.
items.example: I get what you're saying about the need for more resources, it's a valid concern.
items.plain: I understand your point about the need for more resources, it's a valid concern.
items.note: A common, informal way to indicate comprehension and often, agreement.

items.meaning: Expresses complete and enthusiastic agreement with someone's statement.
items.example: I totally agree that we need to prioritize employee well-being in this company.
items.plain: I completely agree that we need to prioritize employee well-being in this company.
items.note: A common, informal way to express strong agreement.

items.meaning: Expresses doubt or skepticism about an idea, argument, or plan.
items.example: They say the new strategy will boost sales, but I'm not convinced it will work.
items.plain: They say the new strategy will boost sales, but I doubt it will work.
items.note: A polite way to express skepticism or partial disagreement.

items.meaning: Expresses skepticism or uncertainty about the likelihood or truth of something.
items.example: He promised to finish the project by tomorrow, but I have my doubts.
items.plain: He promised to finish the project by tomorrow, but I'm not sure he will.
items.note: A common way to express personal skepticism or lack of confidence.

items.meaning: Expresses dissatisfaction or mild annoyance about a situation.
items.example: The decision to cut our training budget, I'm not happy about that at all.
items.plain: The decision to cut our training budget, I'm very dissatisfied with that at all.
items.note: A direct, but polite, way to express displeasure.

items.text: That's a bit much to ask
items.form: That's a bit much to ask
items.meaning: Expresses that a request or expectation is unreasonable or excessive.
items.example: Expecting us to work overtime every day this week, that's a bit much to ask.
items.plain: Expecting us to work overtime every day this week, that's an unreasonable request.
items.note: A polite way to indicate that a request is unfair or goes beyond reasonable limits.

items.text: I'm sorry to hear that happened
items.form: I'm sorry to hear that happened
items.meaning: Expresses sympathy or regret for an unfortunate event that occurred.
items.example: I'm sorry to hear that happened with your car; that's really inconvenient.
items.plain: I feel bad that happened with your car; that's really inconvenient.
items.note: A common and empathetic way to respond to someone sharing a negative experience.

items.text: I'm sorry to bother you with this
items.form: I'm sorry to bother you with this
items.meaning: A polite apology for bringing a potentially troublesome issue to someone's attention.
items.example: I'm sorry to bother you with this, but the payment hasn't gone through yet.
items.plain: Please excuse me for troubling you with this, but the payment hasn't gone through yet.
items.note: Used when presenting a problem or request that might be inconvenient for the other person.

items.meaning: Expresses an apology for an error or oversight made by the speaker.
items.example: I'm sorry for my mistake in the report; I'll correct it immediately.
items.plain: I apologize for my error in the report; I'll correct it immediately.
items.note: A direct and common way to apologize for a personal error.

items.text: I'm sorry if I offended you
items.form: I'm sorry if I offended you
items.meaning: Expresses a conditional apology, acknowledging potential offense caused.
items.example: I'm sorry if I offended you with my direct feedback; that wasn't my intention.
items.plain: I apologize if my direct feedback caused offense; that wasn't my intention.
items.note: A polite way to apologize when unsure if offense was taken, or to soften directness.

items.text: I'm sorry to keep you waiting
items.form: I'm sorry to keep you waiting
items.meaning: Expresses an apology for causing someone to wait.
items.example: I'm sorry to keep you waiting; the previous meeting ran over schedule.
items.plain: I apologize for making you wait; the previous meeting ran over schedule.
items.note: A standard polite apology for lateness or causing a delay for someone.

items.meaning: Expresses happiness or satisfaction about one's presence at an event or location.
items.example: After a long journey, I'm glad to be here and finally relax.
items.plain: After a long journey, I'm happy to be here and finally relax.
items.note: A common and polite expression of contentment upon arrival or participation.

items.meaning: Expresses happiness upon meeting or seeing someone.
items.example: Oh, I didn't expect you here! I'm glad to see you.
items.plain: Oh, I didn't expect you here! I'm happy to see you.
items.note: A common and warm greeting, especially when seeing someone unexpectedly or after a while.

items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction that a situation or plan had a successful outcome.
items.example: Despite the initial challenges, I'm glad it worked out in the end.
items.plain: Despite the initial challenges, I'm happy it was successful in the end.
items.note: A common expression of relief and satisfaction after a successful resolution.

items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction that a conversation took place, often resolving an issue.
items.example: I'm glad we talked about the project concerns; I feel much clearer now.
items.plain: I'm happy we discussed the project concerns; I feel much clearer now.
items.note: A common phrase used to conclude a conversation, especially one that was important or difficult.

items.meaning: Expresses relief and happiness that someone is safe or well after a potential danger.
items.example: I heard about your accident, but I'm glad you're okay.
items.plain: I heard about your accident, but I'm relieved you're safe.
items.note: A common and sincere expression of relief for someone's well-being.

items.meaning: Expresses happiness or relief about receiving specific information.
items.example: I'm glad to know that the new security measures are already in place.
items.plain: I'm happy to know that the new security measures are already in place.
items.note: A common and polite way to acknowledge useful or reassuring information.

items.text: I'm glad to hear from you
items.form: I'm glad to hear from you
items.meaning: Expresses happiness upon receiving communication from someone.
items.example: It's been a while! I'm glad to hear from you, how have things been?
items.plain: It's been a while! I'm happy to receive your communication, how have things been?
items.note: A common and warm greeting, especially in written communication or after a long silence.

items.text: I'm glad to be of assistance
items.form: I'm glad to be of assistance
items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to help after providing aid.
items.example: If you need anything else, just ask. I'm glad to be of assistance.
items.plain: If you need anything else, just ask. I'm happy to help.
items.note: A polite and slightly formal phrase used by someone who has provided help.

items.meaning: Expresses satisfaction and willingness to assist after providing aid.
items.example: I'm glad to have helped you with your presentation; it looks great now.
items.plain: I'm happy that I was able to assist you with your presentation; it looks great now.
items.note: A polite and common phrase used by someone who has provided assistance.

items.text: I'm glad to have met you
items.form: I'm glad to have met you
items.meaning: Expresses pleasure at having made someone's acquaintance.
items.example: It was a very insightful discussion. I'm glad to have met you.
items.plain: It was a very insightful discussion. I'm happy that I met you.
items.note: A polite and common phrase used at the end of a first meeting.

i'm glad to be of assistance.note: Checker slip: The key accurately describes the expression's meaning as a polite statement of pleasure in helping.
